text.p: The U.S. raid on Iraq left commodity markets outside the petroleum sector unmoved on Tuesday.
The Commodities Research Bureau index closed 0.48 points lower at 248.98.

Gold either no longer enjoyed its traditional role as a "safe haven" in time of tension, or investors weren't worried enough about events in the Middle East to feel they needed one. Either way, the bullion price edged up about 50 cents an ounce on early buying in Asia then eased to fix in the London afternoon at $386.60 -- hardly changed from Monday.

Copper prices pushed higher during Tuesday afternoon LME trading to challenge the upper end of a new chart band, but other metals lacked appetite, closing mixed. A brief spell of consolidation in mid-afternoon was ended by a flurry of covering, although solid resistance at $2,050 choked this off. Last three months business was at $2,040 a tonne, up $14 from Monday's kerb close.

Movements were less extreme in the rest of the complex, with aluminium mostly content to hold above $1,500. Traders expect the market to stay within a broader $1,470/1,530 band, with last kerb trade today at $1,505, a $5 loss.
Nickel prices flipped higher during the afternoon rings, with buy-stops above $7,500 carrying the market up to $7,600 at one point before last trade at $7,550, a $135 gain from Monday.
Lead attempted to push higher this afternoon, but faltered at the $820 level. However, prices still closed with modest gains with final business at $819, up $4.
The zinc market hardly budged from Monday levels, fluctuating aimlessly in a narrow band with last trade at $1,033, down $2 from yesterday's kerb close.
Tin also stayed close to previous closing levels, concluding the kerb at $6,250 against Monday's $6,250/6,260. The alloy market was indicated at a slightly softer $1,290/1,295 a tonne.

Benchmark Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) wheat futures were scarely changed on the day at around $4.50 a bushel, down from a record $7.50 in March during a "spike" that followed drought in Australia, Russia and North Africa. Another trader said there had been more talk than actual deals on selling grain to Iraq amid arguments over how the U.N. accord would perform.

NYMEX crude oil prices ended sharply higher, as did refined products, on news that the United Nations suspended the Iraqi oil-for-food exchange, but some traders said crude's price was now overextended.
October crude closed up $1.15 to $23.40 a barrel, after reaching a contract high of $24.25 during the day.
"Most of the value gained today was ultimately from the fact we will not see 700,000 barrels a day of oil from the deal any time soon," a trader said.
CSCE world sugar futures ended sharply higher Tuesday, mostly on fund buying on a breakout of a six week 11.40-12.00 cent a lb range for the October contract, traders said.

"The move looked awfully technical in nature, led by fund buying, and does not appear to have much immediate support from the fundamentals, apart from some concern about possible hurricane damage to the domestic U.S. crop," Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes said.

CSCE October world sugar ended up 0.40 cent at 12.18 cents, after seeing an intraday high at 12.20 cents. October sugar saw its highest level since January 1995, when it saw a contract high at 12.50 cents.
Last trades or bids for key Australian-interest commodities.
